Besides, in the case of an application for registration the burden of proof is on the applicant but in the case of rectification proceedings the burden of proof is on the applicant who seeks to rectify or vary the register. In considering the opposition, the requirement of sections 6, 8, 10 are to be fulfilled by the applicant whereas in an application for rectification if filed after seven years of registration as in the present case, the registration can only be attacked on the ground of fraud or if it offends the provisions of section 8(a) of the Act and that too by an aggrieved person within the meaning of the section. Thus, it is clear that the causes of action are altogether different and the relief provided for in the respective cases are also different. 

 17. Now let us advert to the merits of the case. From the pleadings it appears that the petitioner has made out a case both of fraud and of violation of provisions of section 8(a) of the Act. The admitted position is that the mark of the present petitioner had been registered on 11-8-76 whereas the mark of the opposite party No. 2 was registered on 5-5-94 and on 11-8-98 the present petitioner has renewed his mark for another 15 years which is in operation now. Therefore, the rejection of the opposition case on merit is not at all relevant in determining the issue involved in this case. It appears that the opposite party No. 2 obtained the registration of his mark by committing a fraud upon the opposite party No. 1 as the mark of opposite party No. 2 is identical to the mark of the present petitioner and it has been registered as back as on 11-8-76 and that was in his Registry and the law casts a duty upon the Registrar to scrutinise the record before publication of advertisement to see if any similar mark already exists in the Registry. It appears that the Registrar has utterly failed to discharge his obligation before publication of the mark of opposite party No. 2 in the Trade Marks Journal which shows that the Registrar has discharged his duties in a very negligent way and was also utterly negligent in discharging his legal obligation cast upon him by the Act. Be that as it may, it appears that the case of fraud has been established beyond any shadow of doubt. It has been submitted by Mr Islam that both the marks are before this Court and if the Court compares the marks which are identical to each other then the fraud would apparently be established and there is no dispute between the parties that both the marks are identical to each other and the opposite party No. 2 adopted the registered mark of the petitioner which was registered as back as in 1976 and in adopting the mark of the petitioner the opposite party No.2 used the photograph of the son of the petitioner as the photograph of the son of the opposite party No.2. The case of fraud is established beyond any shadow of doubt. Besides, since the opposite party No. 2 has adopted the registered mark of the petitioner, which are identical to each other, it offends the provisions of section 8(a) of the Act. Therefore, section 24 of the Act has no manner of application to the instant case. Mr Hossain, however, in the course of his argument submitted that the petitioner has failed to adduce any evidence to establish any act of deception due to the adoption of the identical mark of the petitioner by the opposite party No. 2 but it is found from the materials on record that the petitioner pays Taka 17 crore over year as tax to the Government whereas the opposite party No. 2 pays only Taka one lac as tax per year and it is also on record that both the petitioner and the opposite party No. 2 carry on their business within the district of Bogra. Therefore, the case of deception is made out because the opposite party No. 1 has accorded registration of "Aziz Biri" of the label, colour, get-up, design and human bust of the petitioner's son named Aziz to the petitioner as back as on 11-8-1976 and subsequently, accorded trade mark registration of identical colour, design, get-up and human bust of petitioner's son in favour of the opposite party No. 2 on 13-12-1998 and the mark of opposite party No. 2 has no separate and distinctive feature. Even if we ignore this aspect of the case then also law is that in order to bring a case within section 8(a) of the Act actual deception need not be proved if the adopted mark is liable to cause confusion or deception to the consumers. Since admittedly the opposite party No. 2 has adopted the identical mark of the petitioner which is identical in all respects, there is every likelihood that the illiterate, indigenous consumers will be confused or deceived by the adoption of the registered mark of the petitioner and that is sufficient to sustain the application. On a comparison of the two marks I am led to the conclusion that since the opposite party No. 2 has adopted the trade mark "Aziz Biri" misrepresenting the actual "Aziz Biri" in similar get-up, packet, colour, size and design of the mark of the petitioner as his trade mark there is every likelihood of deception or confusion to be caused amongst the consumers. It must be remembered that most of the consumers of this product are illiterate people of the country, that is, most of the consumers of this product have no knowledge of letters and they identify the product by the mark. In the instant case both the marks, that is, the mark of the petitioner and the opposite party No. 2. are identical to each other and it is also an established fact that the mark of the petitioner is a prior registered mark. Therefore, there is every likelihood that the consumers will be deceived by the mark of the opposite party No. 2 and it brooks no controversy to say that the poor consumers are being deceived by the opposite party No. 2 and selling his goods as the goods of the petitioner. Thus, it appears to me that in the instant application the petitioner has been able to substantiate the allegation of fraud as well as the violation of the provision of section 8(a) of the Act. Besides, Mr Hossain has relied on the decision reported in PLD 1999 Karachi 281 and I have carefully gone through the decision as best as I could do and I find that that case does not at all help Mr Hossain rather it cuts at the root of the case of the opposite party No.2. In that case the first legal proposition which has been laid down is that a petition for rectification of trade mark can be made under section 46 of the Act either to the Registrar or to the High Court and if the application for rectification is made to the Registrar no second application under section 46 lies to the High Court. Secondly, it was held that the provision of section 46 is independent of section 76. Therefore, in case a petitioner invokes the jurisdiction of the High Court under section 46 of the Act for rectification, then the remedy of appeal under section 76 will not be available to him. But if the Registrar is approached by an aggrieved person under section 46 of the Act, then in case if the decision is not acceptable to him, he would be entitled to invoke section 76 by filing appeal before the High Court. It was further held in that case that the term "person aggrieved" should be liberally interpreted and that burden of a petitioner is not so onerous to prove himself to be aggrieved but if he, prima facie, shows that there exists similarity in the trade mark registered and his trade mark and that there is every likelihood of deception or confusion, it will suffice to give him a right to maintain a petition. Finally, discussing the legal provisions the Karachi High Court observed that the registration of the mark even after the lapse of 7 years does not attain any finality because it is liable to be challenged under section 46 Of the Act provided that he can bring his case within the ambit of section 24 of the Act and the Karachi High Court went one step further and said that once it is found that the case is attracted by the provision of the Act then in dealing with an application under section 46 the Court is also competent not only to look into the section 8(a) but also to section 10 of the Act.
